embodied-ai: A clear editorial-style illustration of a service robot in a small grocery shop, shown as one integrated sensing-to-action system: a customer gives a spoken request, “Please get the red tea,” while sound waves travel toward the robot’s microphone; its camera view overlays identify several nearly identical tea boxes, including one partly hidden behind another item; arrows connect microphone and cameras to a visible internal AI decision map, then down to the robot’s motors and gripper as it carefully reaches for the correct box. Around it, everyday complications make the physical challenge visible—a child and shopping trolley move nearby, a dropped item lies in the aisle, shelves are slightly disordered, and a safety-zone path curves around people and obstacles—contrasting the simple speech bubble with the complex, cautious real-world perception and action required to fulfil it.
humanoid-robot: A clear editorial-style cutaway scene in a familiar workplace that blends a shop, warehouse and kitchen: at the center, a plainly mechanical humanoid robot with torso, head, two articulated arms, hands and slightly bent legs stands beside a human-height counter and shelving, reaching for a jar by its handle while carrying a box, showing why its body fits tools and spaces made for people; visible overlays reveal cameras and depth sensors noticing a nearby worker, internal perception software mapping objects and people, and control signals running to motors in its joints and fingers. Around it, a tipped object, a crowded aisle and uneven floor markings suggest the hard challenges of balance, safe movement and grasping varied items, while a wheeled non-humanoid machine in the background cannot easily reach the same shelf, emphasizing that human shape is useful but not sufficient for general capability.
retail-automation: A clear cutaway illustration of a modern grocery shop operating as a connected system: at the front, customers use self-checkout kiosks and a vending-style pickup locker, with one shopper scanning an item successfully while another faces a payment-error screen and presses a prominent “help” button; a nearby human employee assists them, showing that automation does not eliminate staff. Across the aisles, a shelf-stocking robot pauses beside a spilled item, an accessible checkout is usable by a wheelchair user, and electronic shelf labels link by visible data lines to an inventory dashboard. In the background, a warehouse conveyor sorts boxes while a worker restocks a machine, and small visual callouts show practical disruptions—an out-of-stock shelf, a security alert, a jammed scanner, and a robot needing charging—contrasted with smooth flows of goods and data, conveying that retail automation succeeds through reliable operation, maintenance, safety, and human support rather than a single impressive machine.
